title: Explainability and Interpretability
subtitle: What explanations are, how they are made, and when they mislead
overview: Explanations are the usual proposed fix for miscalibrated trust. This stage covers what 'explanation' means to different groups, how popular methods mislead, why an LLM's account of its reasoning may not match its computation, and mechanistic interpretability. You need this to judge explanation studies.

modules.title: What is an explanation?
modules.goal: Explain what social science says about how people explain, the different goals of interpretability, and how to evaluate it.
modules.guide: Read Miller first, focusing on his four main findings. Then read Lipton, who shows 'interpretability' covers several goals, and Doshi-Velez and Kim on evaluating it. Key terms: interpretability (how well a person can understand why a model acted); transparency (understanding the model's internals); post-hoc explanation (explaining an output without opening the model); contrastive explanation (answering 'why P rather than Q?'); explainee (who receives the explanation).

resources.title: Explanation in Artificial Intelligence: Insights from the Social Sciences
resources.authors: Tim Miller
resources.why: Grounds XAI in social science research on how people actually explain things.
resources.focus: Sections 1 and 2, including the four major findings; skim the rest and read the conclusion.

resources.title: The Mythos of Model Interpretability
resources.authors: Zachary C. Lipton
resources.why: Shows 'interpretable' names several different goals, so always ask which one a paper means.

resources.title: Towards A Rigorous Science of Interpretable Machine Learning
resources.authors: Finale Doshi-Velez, Been Kim
resources.why: Gives the standard three-level taxonomy for evaluating interpretability, which HAI studies use to describe their designs.
resources.focus: Sections 1-3, especially the taxonomy of evaluation approaches.

quiz.q: According to Miller, explanations people give are typically 'contrastive'. What does that mean?
choices: They contrast the model with competing models
They answer why one outcome happened rather than some other expected outcome
They use high-contrast visuals
They list every possible cause
quiz.explain: Miller's first finding: people ask 'why P rather than Q?', where Q is often implicit. An explanation that ignores the user's expected alternative may not answer their actual question.

quiz.q: Which of these is one of Miller's main findings about human explanation?
choices: People want every contributing cause listed
Statistical probabilities are the most satisfying explanations
People select a small number of causes from many possible ones, and probabilities matter less than causes
Explanations are the same no matter who receives them
quiz.explain: Miller reports that explanations are selected (people pick one or two causes using biases), that probabilities matter less than causal stories, and that explanations are social, tailored to the explainee.

quiz.q: What does Miller mean by calling explanations 'social'?
choices: They are a transfer of knowledge in a conversation, shaped by what the explainer believes the explainee knows
They should be posted on social media
They must be written by a group
They are only about social topics
quiz.explain: Miller treats explanation as part of a conversation between explainer and explainee. This is why a single fixed explanation for every user often falls short.

quiz.q: Lipton separates two broad families of interpretability. What are they?
choices: Global and local accuracy
Supervised and unsupervised
Fast and slow
Transparency (understanding how the model works) and post-hoc interpretability (explaining its outputs after the fact)
quiz.explain: Lipton lists transparency at the level of the whole model, its components and its training algorithm, versus post-hoc methods such as text explanations, visualizations, local explanations and explanation by example.

quiz.q: Which claim does Lipton make about linear models?
choices: They are always perfectly interpretable
They are not automatically more interpretable than deep networks, for example when they rely on many heavily engineered features
They should never be used
They are always less accurate than deep networks
quiz.explain: Lipton challenges the common assumption that linear models are interpretable by default; it depends on which notion of interpretability you mean and on the inputs.

quiz.q: A team tests explanations by having radiologists use them during their real diagnostic work. In Doshi-Velez and Kim's taxonomy this is:
choices: Functionally-grounded evaluation
Human-grounded evaluation
Application-grounded evaluation
Proxy evaluation
quiz.explain: Application-grounded means real users on the real task. Human-grounded uses real people on simplified tasks; functionally-grounded uses no humans, only a formal proxy for interpretability.

quiz.q: Why, according to Doshi-Velez and Kim, is interpretability needed at all?
choices: Because some goals, such as safety or fairness, cannot be fully written into the model's objective, leaving an incompleteness that humans must check
Because all models are inaccurate
Because regulations require it in every country
Because users enjoy explanations
quiz.explain: They argue the need arises from incompleteness in how the problem is formalized: when we cannot fully specify what we want, we need to inspect how the model reaches its outputs.

modules.exercise: Take one output from an AI product you use, such as a loan decision or a recommendation. Write three explanations for it: a feature-based one, a contrastive one in Miller's sense, and an example-based one. Then say which of Doshi-Velez and Kim's evaluation levels you would use to compare them, and why.

modules.title: Explanation techniques and their limits
modules.goal: Explain how LIME, SHAP and Integrated Gradients work, how sanity checks expose misleading explanations, and Rudin's case for interpretable models.
modules.guide: Start with Molnar's chapters, then LIME and SHAP. Integrated Gradients adds axioms attribution should satisfy. Adebayo et al. show some saliency maps barely depend on the model. Rudin opposes explaining black boxes in high-stakes decisions. Key terms: feature attribution (credit per input feature); local explanation (one prediction); surrogate model (simple local imitator); Shapley value (game-theory payoff split); saliency map (pixels that mattered); baseline (reference input, e.g., a black image).

resources.title: Interpretable Machine Learning
resources.authors: Christoph Molnar
resources.why: A free textbook with clear, non-mathematical chapters on each explanation method.
resources.focus: The linked LIME chapter, then the SHAP and Saliency Maps chapters.

resources.title: "Why Should I Trust You?": Explaining the Predictions of Any Classifier
resources.authors: Marco Tulio Ribeiro, Sameer Singh, Carlos Guestrin
resources.why: Introduces LIME, a widely used method, with user studies on whether explanations help people judge models.
resources.focus: Sections 1-3 (the method) and the user experiments, including husky versus wolf.

resources.title: A Unified Approach to Interpreting Model Predictions
resources.authors: Scott Lundberg, Su-In Lee
resources.why: Explains what SHAP, the most widely deployed attribution method in industry, guarantees.
resources.focus: Sections 1-3: additive feature attribution methods and the three properties. Skim estimation methods.

resources.title: Axiomatic Attribution for Deep Networks
resources.authors: Mukund Sundararajan, Ankur Taly, Qiqi Yan
resources.why: Introduces Integrated Gradients and judging attribution methods by axioms, not by plausible-looking output.
resources.focus: Sections 1-3 (the two axioms and the method).

resources.title: Sanity Checks for Saliency Maps
resources.authors: Adebayo, Gilmer, Muelly, Goodfellow, Hardt, Kim
resources.why: Shows a convincing-looking explanation can reveal almost nothing about the model, a key caution for user studies.
resources.focus: Sections 1-3 and the randomization test figures.

resources.title: Stop Explaining Black Box Machine Learning Models for High Stakes Decisions and Use Interpretable Models Instead
resources.authors: Cynthia Rudin
resources.why: Argues against post-hoc explanation in high-stakes settings such as criminal justice and healthcare.

quiz.q: How does LIME explain a single prediction?
choices: It reads the model's weights directly
It retrains the model on a smaller dataset
It perturbs the input, queries the black-box model on those variations, and fits a simple, interpretable model weighted toward samples close to the original input
It asks a human expert to annotate the input
quiz.explain: LIME is model-agnostic: it only needs to query the model. The simple surrogate is meant to be faithful locally, near that input, not across the whole model.

quiz.q: In LIME's husky-versus-wolf experiment, what did the explanations reveal?
choices: The classifier was relying on snow in the background rather than on the animal
The classifier was perfect
Huskies and wolves are genetically identical
Users preferred no explanations
quiz.explain: Ribeiro et al. deliberately trained a flawed classifier in which wolf photos had snow. Explanations helped participants see the model was untrustworthy and identify snow as the feature it used.

quiz.q: What do Lundberg and Lee prove about SHAP values?
choices: They are the fastest attributions to compute
Within the class of additive feature attribution methods, Shapley values are the unique solution satisfying local accuracy, missingness and consistency
They always match human intuition
They work only for linear models
quiz.explain: The paper unifies several earlier methods, including LIME, as additive feature attributions and shows that only Shapley values satisfy the three properties. These are mathematical guarantees, not guarantees that users will understand them.

quiz.q: Integrated Gradients satisfies 'completeness'. What does that mean?
choices: Every pixel receives a positive attribution
The method explains every model in existence
Attributions are computed for every training example
The attributions add up to the difference between the model's output on the input and its output on the baseline
quiz.explain: Integrated Gradients accumulates gradients along a straight path from a baseline (such as a black image) to the input, so attributions sum to the output difference. The choice of baseline therefore affects the explanation.

quiz.q: What did Adebayo et al.'s model-randomization test show for some popular saliency methods, such as Guided Backpropagation?
choices: Their maps changed completely when the model's weights were randomized
Their maps looked much the same even after the model's weights were randomized, so they were not reflecting what the model had learned
They became more accurate on random models
They could not be computed on random models
quiz.explain: If an explanation barely changes when the model is destroyed, it cannot be telling you about the model. Adebayo et al. compare such methods to edge detectors, while plain gradients and GradCAM passed the test.

quiz.q: What is Rudin's main recommendation?
choices: For high-stakes decisions, use inherently interpretable models instead of explaining black boxes after the fact
Always use the most accurate black box and add SHAP
Avoid machine learning in high-stakes settings entirely
Explanations should be written by lawyers
quiz.explain: Rudin argues that post-hoc explanations of black boxes can be unfaithful and that the assumed trade-off between accuracy and interpretability often does not hold for structured data, using criminal-justice risk prediction as an example.

quiz.q: Clinicians in a study say a saliency map 'looks reasonable'. Based on Adebayo et al., why is that not enough?
choices: Clinicians cannot read images
Saliency maps are always wrong
Looking plausible to people does not show that the map depends on what the model learned; sanity checks are needed
Saliency maps cannot be shown to users
quiz.explain: Adebayo et al. warn that visual inspection alone can be misleading, because some maps look plausible even for a randomized model.

modules.exercise: Design a user study testing whether SHAP explanations improve appropriate reliance (not just trust) on a loan-approval model. Include a condition with a deliberately flawed model, as in LIME's husky-versus-wolf experiment. State what pattern of results would show that explanations help, and what pattern would show they merely increase trust.

modules.title: Human-centered XAI
modules.goal: Explain how HCI researchers design and evaluate explanations around users' questions, and why faithfulness differs from plausibility.
modules.guide: Liao, Gruen and Miller start from what users ask. Wang et al. link human reasoning theories to XAI techniques. Kulesza et al. let users correct the model. Jacovi and Goldberg separate convincing from accurate. Ehsan and Riedl (optional) add social context. Key terms: XAI question bank (typical user questions); counterfactual explanation (what change flips the outcome); faithfulness (matches the model's real reasoning); plausibility (seems convincing); sociotechnical (technology plus people, institutions).

resources.title: Questioning the AI: Informing Design Practices for Explainable AI User Experiences
resources.authors: Q. Vera Liao, Daniel Gruen, Sarah Miller
resources.why: Provides the XAI question bank, a widely used tool for designing explanations around user needs.
resources.focus: The method (practitioner interviews), the question bank table, and the design implications.

resources.title: Designing Theory-Driven User-Centric Explainable AI
resources.authors: Danding Wang, Qian Yang, Ashraf Abdul, Brian Y. Lim
resources.why: Links theories of human reasoning and cognitive biases to XAI techniques, applied in a clinical tool.
resources.focus: The conceptual framework figure, the section on mitigating cognitive biases, and the clinical case study.

resources.title: Principles of Explanatory Debugging to Personalize Interactive Machine Learning
resources.authors: Todd Kulesza, Margaret Burnett, Weng-Keen Wong, Simone Stumpf
resources.why: Treats explanation as a two-way loop: the system explains itself and the user corrects it.
resources.focus: The explainability and correctability principles, the EluciDebug prototype, and the main results.

resources.title: Towards Faithfully Interpretable NLP Systems: How should we define and evaluate faithfulness?
resources.authors: Alon Jacovi, Yoav Goldberg
resources.why: Separates faithfulness from plausibility, a distinction every HAI study of explanations must respect.
resources.focus: Sections 1-3, including the guidelines for evaluating faithfulness.

resources.title: Human-centered Explainable AI: Towards a Reflective Sociotechnical Approach
resources.authors: Upol Ehsan, Mark O. Riedl
resources.why: Argues XAI must understand who the human is, including their values and social context.

quiz.q: How did Liao, Gruen and Miller gather their findings?
choices: A large online survey of end users
Interviews with 20 UX and design practitioners working on AI products, using an XAI question bank as a probe
Benchmarking explanation algorithms
Eye tracking of radiologists
quiz.explain: The paper interviews practitioners to find gaps between XAI algorithms and product needs, and uses the question bank as a study probe.

quiz.q: A loan applicant asks: 'What would I need to change to get approved?' Which category of Liao et al.'s question bank is this?
choices: Performance
Data
How to be that (a counterfactual question about getting a different outcome)
How (global model logic)
quiz.explain: The question bank separates 'Why', 'Why not', 'What if', 'How to be that', 'How to still be this' and others. Asking how to reach a different outcome is 'How to be that', answered by counterfactual explanations.

quiz.q: What do Wang et al. contribute beyond proposing a framework?
choices: A new deep learning architecture
A proof that explanations always reduce bias
A benchmark of saliency methods
An explainable clinical diagnostic tool for intensive care, built using the framework and examined in a co-design exercise with clinicians
quiz.explain: Wang et al. draw on philosophy and psychology to link reasoning processes and cognitive biases to XAI features, then apply the framework in a clinical prototype.

quiz.q: Kulesza et al.'s Explanatory Debugging has two core principles. Which pair is it?
choices: Explainability and correctability
Accuracy and speed
Privacy and fairness
Simplicity and novelty
quiz.explain: The system should explain its reasoning (iteratively, soundly and completely, without overwhelming the user) and let users correct it in actionable, reversible ways that are always honored.

quiz.q: According to Jacovi and Goldberg, what is the difference between faithfulness and plausibility?
choices: They are two names for the same property
Faithfulness is about how convincing an explanation is; plausibility is about accuracy
Faithfulness is how accurately an explanation reflects the model's actual reasoning; plausibility is how convincing it is to humans
Plausibility applies only to images
quiz.explain: An explanation can be highly plausible and completely unfaithful. The two must be evaluated separately.

quiz.q: Why do Jacovi and Goldberg advise against using human ratings to evaluate faithfulness?
choices: Humans are too slow
Human ratings measure how plausible an explanation seems, not whether it reflects the model's real reasoning
Human ratings are always biased toward negative scores
Ethics boards forbid it
quiz.explain: People cannot see inside the model, so their judgments reflect plausibility. Faithfulness needs tests against the model itself.

quiz.q: What do Ehsan and Riedl argue Human-centered XAI must understand more fully?
choices: 'Who' the human is, including their values, interpersonal dynamics and the social setting of the AI system
The exact gradient of each layer
How to remove humans from decision loops
The hardware the model runs on
quiz.explain: Ehsan and Riedl call for a reflective, sociotechnical approach that draws on methods such as value-sensitive and participatory design.

modules.exercise: Pick one category from Liao et al.'s question bank (for example 'Why not'). For a concrete AI product, choose an explanation technique from the previous module that could answer it. Then describe two separate evaluations: one testing faithfulness without human judges, and one testing usefulness with real users, following Jacovi and Goldberg's distinction.

modules.title: Do LLMs explain themselves faithfully?
modules.goal: Explain the evidence that chain-of-thought explanations can be unfaithful, how faithfulness is tested, and what it means for users.
modules.guide: In chain-of-thought, the model reasons before answering. Turpin et al. show it can omit what drove the answer. Lanham et al. tamper with the reasoning to test faithfulness. Chen et al. test reasoning models. Kadavath et al. (optional) study model self-knowledge. Key terms: unfaithful explanation (plausible but not the real cause); biasing feature (prompt cue pushing an answer); post-hoc rationalization (justifying a chosen answer); calibration (confidence matching accuracy).

resources.title: Language Models Don't Always Say What They Think: Unfaithful Explanations in Chain-of-Thought Prompting
resources.authors: Miles Turpin, Julian Michael, Ethan Perez, Samuel R. Bowman
resources.why: Direct evidence that the reasoning an LLM shows users can omit the real reason for its answer.
resources.focus: Sections 1-3 and the main results figure; note the social-bias experiments.

resources.title: Measuring Faithfulness in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
resources.authors: Lanham, Chen, Radhakrishnan, Steiner, et al.
resources.why: Introduces intervention tests for chain-of-thought faithfulness and finds it varies with task and model size.
resources.focus: Sections 1-2 (the interventions) and the results on model size.

resources.title: Reasoning Models Don't Always Say What They Think
resources.authors: Chen, Benton, Radhakrishnan, Uesato, et al.
resources.why: Tests whether reasoning models' visible reasoning reveals hint use, which matters for oversight via reasoning traces.
resources.focus: Abstract, introduction and main results on how often hint use is verbalized.

resources.title: Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know
resources.authors: Kadavath, Conerly, Askell, Henighan, et al.
resources.why: Studies whether models can estimate their own correctness, the basis for showing users confidence signals.
resources.focus: Section 1 and the sections introducing P(True) and P(IK).

quiz.q: How did Turpin et al. bias models in their experiments?
choices: By retraining the models on biased data
By adding features to the prompt, such as reordering few-shot answers so the correct one is always '(A)', or having the user suggest an answer
By deleting parts of the model
By translating the questions
quiz.explain: Turpin et al. added biasing cues to the prompt and then checked whether the chain-of-thought explanations mentioned those cues.

quiz.q: What did Turpin et al. find about the explanations models gave under these biases?
choices: The explanations almost always mentioned the bias
The models refused to answer
Accuracy improved
The models' answers shifted toward the biased option, but their explanations rarely mentioned the bias and instead rationalized the answer
quiz.explain: The explanations were plausible but unfaithful: they gave reasons for the biased answer without acknowledging the real influence. On a social-bias task, explanations justified stereotype-aligned answers without mentioning stereotypes.

quiz.q: Which of these is one of Lanham et al.'s tests of chain-of-thought faithfulness?
choices: Truncating the reasoning early or inserting a mistake, and checking whether the final answer changes
Asking users to rate the reasoning
Comparing reasoning length to accuracy
Translating the reasoning to another language
quiz.explain: If the answer does not change when the reasoning is cut short or corrupted, the model was not really relying on that reasoning. Other tests paraphrase the reasoning or replace it with filler tokens.

quiz.q: Why did Lanham et al. replace the chain of thought with filler tokens such as '...'?
choices: To make outputs shorter for users
To test whether any gain comes simply from extra computation over more tokens rather than from the content of the reasoning
To hide the answer
To reduce cost
quiz.explain: Filler tokens give the model more positions to compute with but no reasoning content. They did not reproduce the benefit of chain-of-thought.

quiz.q: What did Lanham et al. find about model size and faithfulness?
choices: Larger models were always more faithful
Size made no difference
On most tasks, larger and more capable models produced less faithful reasoning
Only the smallest models used chain-of-thought
quiz.explain: Lanham et al. report that faithfulness often decreased with scale, suggesting one might choose a smaller model when faithful reasoning matters.

quiz.q: What did Chen et al. (2025) find about reasoning models' chains of thought?
choices: They always disclose when they use a hint
They never use hints
When models used a hint in the prompt, their reasoning often did not mention it; in most settings the reveal rate was below 20%
Reinforcement learning made them perfectly faithful
quiz.explain: The models mentioned hint use in at least some cases, but often in under 20% of them. Outcome-based RL improved faithfulness at first and then plateaued, so reading the chain of thought cannot rule out hidden influences.

quiz.q: From an HAI perspective, why do these findings matter for products that show users the model's reasoning?
choices: Visible reasoning can make answers look justified and raise trust even when it does not reflect the true cause, which can encourage over-reliance
Users never read reasoning traces
Reasoning traces are always faithful for commercial models
Showing reasoning makes models more accurate
quiz.explain: Turpin et al. note that plausible but unfaithful explanations can increase trust without increasing safety, which connects to automation bias and trust calibration from Stage 5.

modules.exercise: Design a user study testing whether showing an LLM's chain of thought changes people's reliance when that reasoning is unfaithful. Use Turpin et al.'s biasing cues to create trials with unfaithful reasoning. What is your dependent measure, what are your conditions, and what result would show that displaying reasoning is harmful?

modules.title: Mechanistic interpretability
modules.goal: Explain the core ideas of mechanistic interpretability (features, circuits, superposition, sparse dictionary learning) and what they reveal about language models.
modules.guide: Start with 'Zoom In', then 'Mathematical Framework' using Stage 3 notes. 'Toy Models of Superposition' explains uninterpretable neurons; Monosemanticity papers fix this with sparse autoencoders. 'Biology of a Large Language Model' is optional. Key terms: feature (represented input property); circuit (features linked into a computation); polysemantic neuron (fires for unrelated things); superposition (more features than dimensions); residual stream (running vector all layers update); sparse autoencoder (rewrites activations as few features).

resources.title: Zoom In: An Introduction to Circuits
resources.authors: Olah, Cammarata, Schubert, Goh, Petrov, Carter
resources.why: Sets out the mechanistic interpretability program accessibly, with many concrete examples.

resources.title: A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits
resources.authors: Elhage, Nanda, Olsson, Henighan, et al.
resources.why: Gives the core tools (residual stream, attention-head circuits, induction heads) used in later Transformer work.
resources.focus: Summary, residual stream, one-layer models, and two-layer induction heads. Skip detailed math at first.

resources.title: Toy Models of Superposition
resources.authors: Elhage, Hume, Olsson, Schiefer, et al.
resources.why: Explains why individual neurons are often uninterpretable, motivating the dictionary-learning methods below.
resources.focus: Introduction, key results summary, and the first superposition demonstration. Skim the geometry sections.

resources.title: Towards Monosemanticity: Decomposing Language Models With Dictionary Learning
resources.authors: Bricken, Templeton, Batson, Chen, et al.
resources.why: Shows sparse autoencoders split a small model's activations into features far more interpretable than neurons.
resources.focus: The results summary, the problem setup, and the detailed investigations of a few features.

resources.title: Scaling Monosemanticity: Extracting Interpretable Features from Claude 3 Sonnet
resources.authors: Templeton, Conerly, Marcus, Lindsey, et al.
resources.why: Scales dictionary learning to a production model, finding abstract, safety-relevant features usable for steering behavior.
resources.focus: Key results, feature examples (including Golden Gate Bridge), feature steering, and safety-relevant features.

resources.title: On the Biology of a Large Language Model
resources.authors: Lindsey, Gurnee, Ameisen, Chen, et al.
resources.why: Traces specific computations in a production model, including a chain-of-thought faithfulness case linked to module 4.
resources.focus: Introduction, then case studies on multi-step reasoning, planning in poems, and chain-of-thought faithfulness.

quiz.q: Which three claims does 'Zoom In' propose?
choices: Neural networks are linear, sparse and small
Features are the fundamental unit of networks; features connected by weights form circuits; similar features and circuits form across different models (universality)
Interpretability is impossible, unnecessary and dangerous
Attention is all you need, scale is all you need, data is all you need
quiz.explain: Olah et al. present these as speculative claims supported by evidence from image models, such as curve detectors and a car detector built from window, body and wheel detectors.

quiz.q: What is a 'polysemantic' neuron, as described in Zoom In?
choices: A neuron that responds to several unrelated things, such as cat faces and fronts of cars
A neuron that never activates
A neuron that processes several languages
A neuron that is duplicated across layers
quiz.explain: Polysemantic neurons make neuron-by-neuron analysis hard. 'Toy Models of Superposition' offers an explanation for why they occur.

quiz.q: In 'A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits', what is an induction head?
choices: The first attention head in every model
A head that only attends to the first token
A head that predicts the next word from word frequencies alone
A mechanism, formed by attention heads in different layers working together, that finds an earlier occurrence of the current token and predicts the token that followed it
quiz.explain: Induction heads complete patterns like '[A][B] ... [A] -> [B]'. They need composition between heads in two layers, which is why they appear in two-layer but not one-layer attention-only models.

quiz.q: What is superposition, according to Elhage et al. (2022)?
choices: Running two models at the same time
Stacking layers on top of each other
A network representing more features than it has dimensions, which works when features are sparse but causes interference
Averaging the weights of several models
quiz.explain: When features rarely occur together, a network can pack many into fewer dimensions. This explains polysemantic neurons: each neuron participates in several features.

quiz.q: What method does 'Towards Monosemanticity' use to find interpretable features?
choices: A sparse autoencoder (dictionary learning) that rewrites a layer's activations as combinations of a larger number of mostly inactive features
Visualizing individual neurons
Removing neurons one at a time
Asking the model to describe itself
quiz.explain: Bricken et al. trained sparse autoencoders on the MLP activations of a one-layer Transformer and found that the learned features were much more interpretable than the neurons.

quiz.q: What did 'Scaling Monosemanticity' show about the features it found in Claude 3 Sonnet?
choices: They only captured simple word frequencies
Many were abstract (multilingual and multimodal), and amplifying or suppressing a feature, such as the Golden Gate Bridge feature, changed the model's behavior
They could not be found in a large model
They were identical to individual neurons
quiz.explain: The paper reports abstract features, features relevant to safety such as deception and sycophancy, and steering experiments showing the features causally affect outputs.

quiz.q: In 'On the Biology of a Large Language Model', what did the authors find when the model wrote rhyming poetry?
choices: It picked rhymes at random
It could not rhyme
It copied poems from training data
It planned ahead, representing candidate rhyming words before writing the line that ends with them
quiz.explain: Lindsey et al. report evidence of planning: the model considered words that would rhyme in advance and built the line toward them, rather than only choosing one word at a time without lookahead.

modules.exercise: Mechanistic interpretability results are usually checked by researchers inspecting features, not by end users. Propose how a finding such as a 'sycophancy' feature in Scaling Monosemanticity could become a signal shown to users, and design an evaluation of whether it improves appropriate reliance. What could make such a signal misleading, given what you learned about faithfulness in this stage?
